effect_estimate.comment: No inferential statistical estimates are reported; figures and tables present ordinal point rankings of policies and thematic counts/summaries of 75 challenges and 99 suggestions from 12 expert interviews.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Across 12 interviewed local water professionals, the highest-ranked current policies enabling resilience were Seattle Public Utilities (SPU) 20-year water system plans and historic watershed land acquisition for water supply, the federal Clean Water Act (1972) alongside CSO, regional wastewater, capital improvement, and asset management plans for wastewater (17 policies identified), and the Combined Sewer Overflow (CSO) Program alongside the 2013 CSO/SSO consent decree, NPDES (1972), and 2009 Stormwater Code for stormwater (19 policies identified). Respondents identified 75 future challenges and 99 suggestions across nine themes: informal rules ('mindset and habits') and 'costs' (rate increases, funding shortages, and maintaining water affordability) ranked as the top two challenge categories, while inflexible water rights and narrow regulatory permits under the CWA/NPDES were reported to hamper integrated thinking, local environmental prioritization, and affordability. Policies enabling resilience were concluded to be most effective when implemented locally alongside supportive multi-level governance and shifts in informal rules.

evidence_quotes.quote: Copyright © 2019 Laura M. Inha, Jarmo J. Hukka
To help address these research gaps, we focus on the resilience of water services from the policy point of view in the case of Seattle, Washington, in the USA.

Based on a literature review and semi-structured interviews among twelve selected local water professionals, this paper a) defines development steps and policies that have led to the current situation; b) explores key policies that are important to the resilience of Seattle’s water services; and c) examines challenges in and recommendations for improving resilience in the future.
The research methods used in this paper are a literature review, policy analysis, and semi-structured interviews.

For water supply, two policies stand out as most important. One is the local, periodically updated, Seattle Public Utilities’ water system plans. These are plans for the regional water supply, water system, shortage response, and demand forecast for at least twenty years.
While broad in scope and important, the Clean Water Act, the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) and associated permits over-prioritize water quality and combined sewer overflows.
